s: A retail company runs a stateless web tier on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. During a recent incident, packet loss in one AZ raised latency for a third of requests. The instances in that AZ still passed their health checks. The company wants AWS to move traffic away from an impaired AZ automatically, with no custom tooling, and wants the remaining AZs to absorb the load without new instances having to launch. Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create an AWS Fault Injection Service experiment that uses the AZ Availability: Power Interruption scenario, and run it whenever latency alarms fire.
Configure Route 53 health checks against per-AZ DNS names of the load balancer, and use failover routing to remove the impaired AZ.

Enable Route 53 ARC zonal autoshift on the ALB and the Auto Scaling group, configure the required practice runs with CloudWatch alarms, and pre-provision enough capacity that any two AZs can carry peak traffic.
Switch the Auto Scaling group to ELB health checks with a shorter grace period so that slow instances are replaced automatically.

w.y: With zonal autoshift, AWS shifts traffic away from an AZ when it detects an impairment, and that catches gray failures that per-instance health checks miss. Pre-provisioning for N-1 AZs makes the shift statically stable. Together these match 'automatically, with no custom tooling' and 'without new instances having to launch'.

o.A: FIS injects faults for testing. It does not remediate a real impairment.
o.B: Per-AZ DNS health checks are custom work. They also probe the load balancer node, which may pass while the targets degrade.
o.C: Correct: zonal autoshift plus N-1 static capacity moves traffic out of the AZ with no control-plane dependency.
o.D: The instances were passing health checks, so tighter health checks would not catch this gray failure, and replacements need new launches.

d: AWS shifts automatically; no new launches needed
